messages.author: b8b584e7eb4a9eeb
messages.subject: ID of individuals between sessions
parts:
Does secr use information of individual animals between sessions if g0 or sigma are shared or modeled for heterogeneity (h2)?

For example. If individual A is captured in sessions 1 and 2, does it need to have the same ID in both sessions?

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: ID of individuals between sessions
parts:
No x2. Detection histories do not connect across sessions. There are currently only minor and exotic exceptions to this statement (one can generate connected data with sim.capthist). Warning: the implicit assumption that each session is a new, independent sample can lead to over-optimistic confidence intervals.
Murray

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: ID of individuals between sessions
parts:
I just meant 'No' is the answer to each of your two questions :-)

Is there a problem? I don't see one. Your code fits constant g0 and sigma across sessions, which may or may not be appropriate. I don't think (g0~1,sigma~h2) is a plausible model. Also, our 2014 paper on compensatory heterogeneity refers to sex-specific sigma and might be useful (Ecology 95:1341-1348).

Murray

messages.subject: Re: ID of individuals between sessions
parts:
We made the argument (and I believe it) that differences in home range size (and hence sigma) should affect g0 (or lambda0 in the HHN parameterization). On the other hand, it is conceivable that g0 might vary independently even when sigma is constant, so (g0~h2, sigma~1) seems meaningful (but not consistent with your observation that sexes differ in home range size, and therefore perhaps not worth considering). The only issue with (g0~h2, sigma~h2) is that it may be more than is needed cf (a0~1, sigma~h2).
Murray

messages.author: 2c49652a5796ed9c
messages.subject: Re: ID of individuals between sessions
parts: I'll just add my 2 cents here.  Compensation between g0 and sigma based on proportional space use makes sense, but other factors influence g0 and could potentially have a larger influence on g0 differences than space use.  For example, male felids have larger sigmas then females, but in camera trap studies where cameras are placed on larger trails, their g0 may be roughly the same as females because they use the larger trails more extensively.  Sure, it's probably not exactly the same, but g0~1 sigma~h2 may be an efficient way to model this.  I'm sure there are cases where some other behavioral difference between groups can mitigate, outweigh, or add to the effects of differential space use.

messages.author: a962fffd7a5358b2
messages.subject: Re: ID of individuals between sessions
parts:
I have two cents more. I suspect there might frequently be little or no compensation between g0 and sigma in the case sex-specific sigma for adults.  Males frequently have larger home ranges than females so that their range includes or overlaps the ranges of several reproductive females.  Males then travel extensively within these large ranges, checking on the reproductive status of, and advertising themselves to, several females, and marking or defending their territory to exclude other males. The large male home range is not about meeting energetic requirements, it's about maximizing reproductive output. Females need to devote energy to gestation, lactation, etc, but more of males' energetic investment into reproduction comes in the form of movement. Therefore, at least at some times of year, males may just as likely to be at any specific location within their large range as females would be within a smaller one (hence no compensation between g0 and sigma). 

In the case of black bears, males have much larger ranges than females and move extensively within those ranges during the breeding season, but after the breeding season both sexes travel extensively in search of food, and the difference in home range size between sexes decreases or disappears (based on unpublished home data from Ontario). During the breeding season, I would not expect much compensation between g0 and sigma, and after the breeding season, I would expect sigma to be similar between sexes (and the assumption that activity centers are fixed suspect).  I haven't reviewed SECR studies of black bears recently enough to back up these claims with sex-specific estimates of model parameters during and after the breeding season!

Eric

messages.subject: Re: ID of individuals between sessions
parts: "Therefore, at least at some times of year, males may just as likely to be at any specific location within their large range as females would be within a smaller one (hence no compensation between g0 and sigma). "

I think this is impossible.  Males can't cover more area without reducing space use in the area already covered.  But since they're moving around their larger home range faster, than females are moving around their smaller home ranges, they may be more likely to be close enough to a trap to smell the bait and be pulled in.  Another consideration is that if you are doing any subsampling of your hair samples, which is common, if larger males deposit more hair samples than smaller females the subsampling process will lower the g0 more for females than males, potentially mitigating or swamping compensation between g0 and sigma from space use.  Or if hair snares are closer to larger trails that the males preferentially use, females with cubs may avoid these areas. 

Based on bear GPS data from KY, I agree that females have reduced space use in the spring and early summer compared to fall, but we saw smaller home ranges for females in all seasons.  But as I'm sure you know, hair snare studies are usually done in the spring to early summer when there is less food on the landscape and hair is easier to snag and this is when the difference is most pronounced.  From my vague memory of bear hair snare studies in the literature and one I worked on recently, I think sigma estimates of males are around 2x that of females.  And SCR is pretty robust to mobile activity centers, at least on well-spaced and regular trapping arrays.  (https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Angela_Fuller3/publication/284358732_Spatial_capture-recapture_models_allowing_Markovian_transience_or_dispersal/links/565340cb08ae4988a7af7c83.pdf)

On Tue, Oct 11, 2016 at 10:39 AM, Eric Howe <ej...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
I have two cents more. I suspect there might frequently be little or no compensation between g0 and sigma in the case sex-specific sigma for adults.  Males frequently have larger home ranges than females so that their range includes or overlaps the ranges of several reproductive females.  Males then travel extensively within these large ranges, checking on the reproductive status of, and advertising themselves to, several females, and marking or defending their territory to exclude other males. The large male home range is not about meeting energetic requirements, it's about maximizing reproductive output. Females need to devote energy to gestation, lactation, etc, but more of males' energetic investment into reproduction comes in the form of movement. Therefore, at least at some times of year, males may just as likely to be at any specific location within their large range as females would be within a smaller one (hence no compensation between g0 and sigma). 

In the case of black bears, males have much larger ranges than females and move extensively within those ranges during the breeding season, but after the breeding season both sexes travel extensively in search of food, and the difference in home range size between sexes decreases or disappears (based on unpublished home data from Ontario). During the breeding season, I would not expect much compensation between g0 and sigma, and after the breeding season, I would expect sigma to be similar between sexes (and the assumption that activity centers are fixed suspect).  I haven't reviewed SECR studies of black bears recently enough to back up these claims with sex-specific estimates of model parameters during and after the breeding season!

Eric

On 10 October 2016 at 11:59, Ben Augustine <baug...@vt.edu> wrote:
I'll just add my 2 cents here.  Compensation between g0 and sigma based on proportional space use makes sense, but other factors influence g0 and could potentially have a larger influence on g0 differences than space use.  For example, male felids have larger sigmas then females, but in camera trap studies where cameras are placed on larger trails, their g0 may be roughly the same as females because they use the larger trails more extensively.  Sure, it's probably not exactly the same, but g0~1 sigma~h2 may be an efficient way to model this.  I'm sure there are cases where some other behavioral difference between groups can mitigate, outweigh, or add to the effects of differential space use.

On Fri, Oct 7, 2016 at 4:41 PM, Murray Efford <murray...@gmail.com> wrote:
We made the argument (and I believe it) that differences in home range size (and hence sigma) should affect g0 (or lambda0 in the HHN parameterization). On the other hand, it is conceivable that g0 might vary independently even when sigma is constant, so (g0~h2, sigma~1) seems meaningful (but not consistent with your observation that sexes differ in home range size, and therefore perhaps not worth considering). The only issue with (g0~h2, sigma~h2) is that it may be more than is needed cf (a0~1, sigma~h2).
Murray

On Sat, Oct 8, 2016 at 9:33 AM, Emiliano Ramalho <eera...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thank you Murray.

Why would (g0~1,sigma~h2) not be plausible? From what I had understood so far sigma would be somewhat proportional to home range size and therefore if sexes have significantly different home range sizes it would be interesting to incorporate that?

Following this same rationale (g0~h2,sigma~h2) is also not and adequate model, right?

Emiliano.

On Fri, Oct 7, 2016 at 4:17 PM, Murray Efford <murray...@gmail.com> wrote:
I just meant 'No' is the answer to each of your two questions :-)

Is there a problem? I don't see one. Your code fits constant g0 and sigma across sessions, which may or may not be appropriate. I don't think (g0~1,sigma~h2) is a plausible model. Also, our 2014 paper on compensatory heterogeneity refers to sex-specific sigma and might be useful (Ecology 95:1341-1348).

Murray


On Sat, Oct 8, 2016 at 9:06 AM, Emiliano Ramalho <eera...@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear Murray, thanks for the prompt reply.

I did no understand what you meant by "No x2".

I have GPS data of the species in the same region of the survey sessions. Males and females have different home range sizes. So I am running the following codes to model this difference. From your reply it made me question if I am running the code correctly.

AllSites.fit1.clip.Sex=secr.fit(allsites, hcov="Sex", model = list(D~session, g0~1, sigma~1), mask = mask_land)

AllSites.fit1.clip.h2Sex=secr.fit(allsites, hcov="Sex", model = list(D~session, g0~h2, sigma~1), mask = mask_land)

AllSites.fit1.clip..h2SEx=secr.fit(allsites, hcov="Sex", model = list(D~session, g0~1, sigma~h2), mask = mask_land)

AllSites.fit1.clip.h2Sex.h2Sex=secr.fit(allsites, hcov="Sex", model = list(D~session, g0~h2, sigma~h2), mask = mask_land)

AIC (AllSites.fit1.clip, AllSites.fit1.clip.h2Sex, AllSites.fit1.clip..h2Sex, AllSites.fit1.clip.h2Sex.h2Sex)

Thanks.






On Thu, Oct 6, 2016 at 5:12 PM, Murray Efford <murray...@gmail.com> wrote:
No x2. Detection histories do not connect across sessions. There are currently only minor and exotic exceptions to this statement (one can generate connected data with sim.capthist). Warning: the implicit assumption that each session is a new, independent sample can lead to over-optimistic confidence intervals.
Murray

On Friday, October 7, 2016 at 3:40:00 AM UTC+13, Emiliano Ramalho wrote:
Does secr use information of individual animals between sessions if g0 or sigma are shared or modeled for heterogeneity (h2)?

For example. If individual A is captured in sessions 1 and 2, does it need to have the same ID in both sessions?
